title: Give My Regards to the Broadway Episode!
summary: Josh and Chuck explore Broadway, the New York theater district and American musical theater. They discuss a listener suggestion (from Sarah Nagy) and start with casual banter about Josh's Broadway trip and buying tickets for Glengarry Glen Ross, plus TKTS day-of booths and ticket prices. The history covers Broadway's origins as a Lenape trail and Dutch-era road, the first recorded play in 1732 (The Recruiting Officer), early musicals like The Beggar's Opera, Oscar Hammerstein I's theaters and the IRT subway, the renaming of Longacre Square to Times Square in 1905, the Shubert brothers, vaudeville and the Ziegfeld Follies, and Irving Berlin and the Gershwins. The hosts then cover the Rodgers and Hammerstein partnership and the book musical, Showboat, West Side Story, Cabaret and the concept musical, Hair, Company, A Chorus Line, Cats, and Phantom of the Opera. Later segments cover Times Square's cleanup and the Disney era with Beauty and the Beast, the 1990s shows Rent and Mamma Mia, Wicked, and Broadway flops such as Moose Murders, Carrie, and Spider-Man: Turn Off the Dark. The episode ends with a listener shout-out from Cody in Raleigh for his mother Bonnie's eightieth birthday and a note that the show inspired two Broadway musicals.

segments.title: Opening banter and Broadway trip
segments.summary: The hosts open with song banter and a listener suggestion from Sarah Nagy. Josh talks about his Broadway trips and buying Glengarry Glen Ross tickets, and they discuss TKTS day-of ticket booths.

segments.title: Broadway ticket prices and show scale
segments.summary: They compare the size of New York Broadway theaters, from the Gershwin at 1,933 seats to the Hayes at 597. They discuss blockbuster productions, special effects, and average ticket prices, with Wicked the most expensive at about $290 on average.

segments.title: Origins of Broadway and early theater
segments.summary: Broadway began as a Lenape tribal trail and was later a Dutch road called Heere Straat. The first recorded play performance was The Recruiting Officer in 1732 at the New Theater on Nassau Street, owned by Governor Rip van Dam. Early musicals included The Beggar's Opera.

segments.title: Oscar Hammerstein I and the theater district
segments.summary: Oscar Hammerstein I, a former cigar factory worker who invented a cigar machine, funded opera houses including the Harlem Opera House and the Olympia in Longacre Square. With the IRT subway, the theater district took shape. Longacre Square was renamed Times Square in 1905 after the New York Times moved there.

segments.title: Shubert brothers, Ziegfeld Follies and early songwriters
segments.summary: The Shubert brothers opened many theaters, and the Schubert Organization still owns seventeen of the forty-one Broadway theaters. The Ziegfeld Follies helped draw everyday audiences. Irving Berlin and George Gershwin wrote famous songs during this era.

segments.title: Rodgers and Hammerstein and the book musical
segments.summary: Oscar Hammerstein II and Jerome Kern created Show Boat, which was integrated but also used blackface. Richard Rodgers and Hammerstein then made Oklahoma! in 1943, which set a performance record of 2,212 performances. Their partnership defined the book musical.

segments.title: West Side Story, Cabaret, Hair and Company
segments.summary: West Side Story in 1957 helped establish the triple threat performer. Cabaret in 1966 introduced the concept musical. Hair in 1968 was an early rock musical. Stephen Sondheim's breakout was Company.

segments.title: A Chorus Line, Cats and Phantom of the Opera
segments.summary: A Chorus Line, a concept musical set in an audition, began a long run in 1975. Cats opened in 1982, and Phantom of the Opera followed in 1988 with elaborate special effects. Phantom holds the record for most performances, at 13,981.

segments.title: Times Square cleanup and Disney era
segments.summary: Times Square was rowdy for decades. Mayors including Koch, Dinkins and Giuliani cleaned it up. John Lindsay offered tax breaks for theaters, and David Dinkins made a deal with Michael Eisner. Disney's Beauty and the Beast opened at the Palace Theatre in 1994.

segments.title: Rent, jukebox musicals and recent hits
segments.summary: Rent in the 1990s tackled heavier topics; Jonathan Larson died before it premiered off Broadway. Mamma Mia! used ABBA songs. The hosts discuss jukebox musicals, Wicked, and Hamilton.

segments.title: Recent Broadway hits and grosses
segments.summary: They discuss Dear Evan Hansen and Wicked's record week, with its five million dollar week in December. The 2023-24 season grossed $1.5 to $1.6 billion with about 12 million attendees across 71 productions and an 89.9 percent average occupancy.

segments.title: Broadway flops
segments.summary: Moose Murders in 1983 closed after one performance. Carrie in 1988 closed after 16 previews and five performances on an eight million dollar budget. Spider-Man: Turn Off the Dark in 2011 had 182 previews and many problems.

segments.title: Previews and critics
segments.summary: The hosts explain Broadway previews, where audiences see shows before opening and critics may review them. They discuss whether critics attend previews.

segments.title: Show inspired by the podcast
segments.summary: The hosts mention a Town and Country article and a producers' email saying the show inspired two Broadway musicals, including Tzacho and Vinzetti.

segments.title: Rare shout-out for Bonnie's 80th birthday
segments.summary: Cody from Raleigh asks for a shout-out for his mother Bonnie Nichols, who listens to the show for companionship after his father died in 2018. The hosts wish her a happy 80th birthday.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: The hosts invite listeners to send stories about the people in their lives by email, and the show credits iHeartRadio.
